          SATOM is mapped to the Network Automation Forum's framework in this release — every MUST requirement met, self-assessed against the pinned upstream commit da82b12; the matrix with every row and its evidence is docs/naf-alignment.md. The upgrade path is unchanged from 3.3.8: the update package accepts a node on 3.3.3 or newer. A node on 3.3.2 or older applies satom-update-3.3.3.tar.gz (release v3.3.3) first, then this one — and on such a node the 3.3.3 package's own update runner must be installed BEFORE applying it (its runner cannot install the wheels the package ships; see Fixed below and docs/offline-update-packages.md §3).

          The upgrade runs migrations wiki04 (Wiki groups merged into Administrator › Access › Groups), wiki05 (comments and subscriptions), wiki06 (Confluence spaces and pages), orch01 (Process event triggers and the key a run was started by) and coll01 (SNMP polling fields on appliances). Nothing new listens or writes by default: the syslog receiver is off until switched on, SNMP polling is opt-in per appliance, an event-triggered Process starts unarmed unless its form says otherwise, and no existing API token gains the new template_draft, template_apply or process_arm capabilities. The one check that is on by default is intent deviation (Settings → Alerts), which compares a bound device with its template and never writes.

          Added

          • The API describes itself, and reads and writes intent and observations — part of "do every phase of the NAF alignment plan". Three things the console had and the API did not:
          • GET /api/v1/openapi.json: an OpenAPI 3.0 document of every route, built at request time from the live router, the scope each view enforces and its docstring. Nothing is kept in a second list, so a route added tomorrow is documented the moment it is registered, and a view without a summary is a test failure rather than an undocumented endpoint.
          • Intent (NAF's name for desired state): GET /templates, /templates/<id> (body, versions, review history, bindings), /bindings, /baselines, scoped to the token's ADOM like a console session. Writing needs two new explicit-only capabilities, in the model of the WAF carve-outs: template_draft creates templates and versions, bindings and baselines and never touches a device; template_apply approves (four-eyes: never the author) and pushes a template through the console's own path — a dry-run preview unless confirm is true, then the canary-gated background job behind the firmware gate. A fleet rollout still needs an approved template and an owner holding Run operations. An empty capability list authorises none of it: a token minted before this release cannot roll a template out.
          • Observability (what SATOM has recorded): GET /appliances/<id>/config-history and config-diff?from=&to= over the Source of Truth, GET /findings (what the alert engine finds now, scoped to the product), and GET /metrics/query, a read-only MetricsQL proxy that accepts only SATOM's own satom_* series, answers within 10 s or says so, and hands a product-bound token only its own devices' series. The metrics store itself stays on loopback with no account of its own; this route is the only way in from outside. The API manual has four new sections (§10–§13); the manual guard now covers every module.
          • Intent deviation: a bound device that no longer matches its template is a finding — phase 3 of the NAF Framework alignment plan, asked as "do every phase of the NAF alignment plan, test each one, then release, document and publish everything". Until now nothing compared desired state with actual state: Config drift says a device changed, and a device that drifted three weeks ago and has been stable since raised nothing while not running what it was bound to. The health engine's new Intent deviation check (on by default, its own toggle and sink family intent) renders each binding's template with the device's variables and compares it, field by field, against the cached device objects — the key-subset diff the approval modal already uses, never equality against a raw snapshot, because an appliance fills in what the template never set. Measured on {device} (7.6.8) and {device} (8.0.6): the appliance answers "4" to a 4, counts its own sub-table rows in sz_* and renumbers *_val handles; those are ignored, and sub-table rows are reported unmeasured rather than guessed at. One warning per binding, keyed intent.<device>:<binding>:<hash> so a corrected device goes quiet and a differently broken one is news; the finding names the fields that differ and never a value, and maintenance and the drift exclude list silence it like drift. The bindings table in the template dialog shows the same verdict as a Compliance column (met / deviates / unmeasured, reason in the tooltip), and hooks can subscribe to the typed event intent.deviation (keys only, no values) beside alert.fired. A template body may now name its collection as the registry logical name, the cmdb tail or the full REST path: all three resolve to the same cached object. In NAF terms this is the Observability block's "event when the actual state differs from the intended one".
          • Processes start from events, on a schedule and from the API; a Compensate step undoes a walk — asked as "do every phase of the NAF alignment plan", the Orchestrator phase: an operator-drawn procedure could only be started by the Run button, nothing could roll a walk back, and no machine could start one. A process now names a trigger event from the integration-hook catalogue (alert.fired, upgrade.failed, change.approved …), narrowed by ADOM, appliance, alert family and a severity floor. The walk is queued as a job the moment the event is noticed and never runs inside the alert evaluation or the hook dispatch that noticed it (those run inside the scheduler's cycle). Three rules bound a storm, each refusal recorded as a run with status skipped and the reason: one running instance per process and appliance, a budget of runs per process per hour (default 10), and rehearsal unless Arm triggered walks is on — which the form says, in red, means SATOM writes with nobody at the screen. A finding that started a walk owes the alert cooldown; one that was skipped does not. Device findings now carry the appliance id (alert.fired payload: appliance_id) so a trigger can point the walk at the device. Walk a process is a new action of the operator catalogue (rehearsal unless its armed parameter is on; an armed walk of a diagram that writes runs only bound to a change request; flagged dangerous, so never through the generic actions API). The new Compensate step undoes what the walk wrote before it, newest first — only the steps that recorded an inverse (a status a catalogue action flipped, an Observatory fix, a provisioning run); a write with no inverse is named unknown, never guessed, and a failed write is never replayed. The inverse travels with the step, so a walk resumed after a manual gate still knows what it wrote. And the API: GET /api/v1/processes, POST /api/v1/processes/<id>/run (rehearsal by default; "armed": true needs the new explicit process_arm capability) and GET /api/v1/process-runs/<id>, under the token's ADOM exactly as the console. Every run carries what started it (trigger_key: the finding key, the scheduled action, the API token).
          • Collection beyond the device APIs: SNMP polling and a syslog receiver — phase 6 of the NAF Framework alignment ("do every phase of the NAF alignment plan, test each one, then release, document and publish everything"). Until now every collector read the appliance's own REST or CLI, and the one log path was a FortiAnalyzer. A new snmp collector polls an appliance over SNMP v2c — sysUpTime, the interface table with its 64-bit byte counters, CPU / memory / disk from the vendor MIB (FortiWeb verified on 7.6.8; the other products' OIDs are the documented ones with HOST-RESOURCES as fallback) — on a client written on the standard library, so the offline bundles carry no new wheel. It is opt-in per appliance: the edit form gains a switch, the port and the community string, stored like the passwords and never shown again; switching it off disables the target rather than leaving a red row. A syslog receiver (UDP and TCP, RFC 3164 / RFC 5424 / the Fortinet key=value body) runs inside the scheduler sidecar on the primary, off by default, bound to 5514 unless told otherwise, and keeps only what known senders say: anything else is dropped and counted. Monitoring → Collection shows both — SNMP per appliance, the receiver's state, counts per device, drops, its settings, and (Global only) the last 500 messages with credential-shaped values blanked. SNMPv3, traps, flows and packet capture are out of scope and the manual says so. The upgrade runs migration coll01 (three columns on appliances).
          • The manual on every node, Documentation Center included — asked as "put the Documentation Center there too", for the sign-in page's Documentation link. That link pointed only at the public site, which a management network often cannot reach; on 2026-10-21 nobody could, with the site's host down. Every node now serves the published pages from its own tree at /manual/: the Documentation Center (its public build, vendored in docs-center/) and the generated reference pages of site/. Documentation opens the Documentation Center, and so does Documentation in the user menu once signed in (the user asked for it next to Profile); API documentation and the AI Advisor's How this works open their reference pages — all on the node, with the public site used only for a page the tree does not carry. What is served is the generators' redacted output, never the Markdown (the routes that rendered docs/*.md stay gone), and nothing outside those two trees or of another file type. Each page's own inline script is admitted by its hash, never by 'unsafe-inline', and nothing is loaded from a third party. Readable without signing in, from every ADOM, and in the container image, which now ships both trees. The release pipeline rebuilds the copy at every cut (step docs_center). On the Concept Map as Documentation Center.
          • Resource history of the SATOM nodes — as asked: "show SATOM's CPU, disk and RAM over time where the system health is, for the secondary node too, and let the API collect this data".
          • Monitoring → SATOM health → Resource history: CPU, memory and disk charts with both nodes on each, over 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 7 days, 30 days or 90 days, with the warning and critical limits from Settings → Thresholds drawn as dashed lines. Until now these readings were a snapshot on the node tiles and were thrown away after each render.
          • Sampled by the existing metrics_scrape action (every 3 minutes) into the local metrics store as satom_node_* series, mirrored to the peer's store, so a promoted standby keeps the history. Its run summary names the node samples, or says why they were not recorded.
          • A node that did not answer leaves a gap and writes satom_node_up 0; its last numbers are never carried forward. A store that did not answer is shown as an error, never as empty charts.
          • API: GET /api/v1/system/nodes (every node now, graded) and GET /api/v1/system/nodes/history (range, node, metrics; 502 store_unavailable when the store does not answer). Read scope, a token bound to the global ADOM, and monitoring on a capability-restricted token. Node addresses are not in the answer. API manual §9.
          • Wiki: comments, following, export and Confluence — the rest of the Wiki plan, as asked: "do the Wiki and Confluence".
          • Comments under every published article, in threads (Reply), in Markdown with the article's own sanitiser. Written by whoever can read the article and holds wiki.write; edited by their author; deleted by their author, the article's author or a moderator (a comment with replies is blanked so the thread still reads). Archived articles keep theirs, closed.
          • Following: an article, a topic (sub-topics included), a tag, an ADOM (its articles and the Global ones), Global, or everything, from a Follow button or Wiki › Following. New versions and comments put a notice in the bell, sent only to people who can open the article at that moment and never to the person who acted. The bell asks again whenever it is drawn, so narrowing an article's audience later hides the notices already sent; deleting an article deletes them. Optional e-mail to the recovery address, one message per person, with the title, description or comment excerpt and the link only.
          • Export of an article's published version (current, or any version from History) as Markdown with a YAML header or as PDF rendered on the node, and of the filtered list as a ZIP of either. Drafts never leave; images are not downloaded into the PDF (SATOM does not fetch an address an author typed).
          • Publish to Confluence, one way: moderators set up spaces (Cloud REST API v2 or Data Center), the credential write-only in the vault or encrypted; the article's author or a moderator publishes its published version, the first time as a new page, then always to that page id with the next version. An article not for everyone needs an explicit acknowledgement, and a credential scan (keys, tokens, FortiOS ENC secrets, passwords in URLs or headers) stops the publication, naming kind and line only; a moderator may override, audited. The calls go through the same checked path as Studio connections (no loopback, link-local, this node or its HA peer; no redirects; credential redacted from errors).
          • SATOM mapped to the NAF Framework — the first step of "do every phase of the NAF alignment plan, test each one, then release, document and publish everything". The Network Automation Forum's vendor-neutral reference model (six functional blocks around the infrastructure; no version number, so SATOM pins upstream commit da82b12, CC0 1.0) now has its own manual page, SATOM and the NAF Framework: why SATOM aligns with it, what SATOM calls each block — the one collision worth knowing is that SATOM's Source of Truth is the framework's Observability, not its Intent — and a conformance matrix, one row per requirement sentence, each with its status and the file that is the evidence. The status line ("mapped to the NAF Framework, with N documented deviations") is derived from the matrix by a test, which also owns the word conformant: no published document may claim it while a MUST row is open. The README, the architecture page of the product site, the engineering, overview, management, API, alerting, CLI-writer, Sentinel and metrics manuals and the user guide say which block each part of SATOM is; the release checklist diffs the upstream framework against the pin at every cut. The framework's diagram and block icons are reproduced unchanged (NOTICE). With the other entries of this release every MUST row of the matrix is met, so the status line reads conformant (self-assessed — the forum issues no certification); three SHOULD/MAY rows stay partial by design.

          Changed

          • Wiki groups are Administrator › Access › Groups, the groups Python Studio apps are shared with: one list of teams instead of two that drift apart. The upgrade merges the Wiki's groups into it (same name in any case = one group, members added together) and keeps every article's audience. Groups are managed by whoever manages users; the Access › Groups page counts the Wiki articles naming each group, and deleting one leaves them closed.

          Fixed

          • One slow scheduled action held the whole scheduler tick. The sidecar runs the due actions one after another, and on 2026-10-21 an HTTP Observatory run over four sites whose host was down took 464 s, during which the deep-monitor sweep, the metrics scrape and the syslog journal's flush all waited. The Observatory now grades an appliance's sites concurrently (four at a time) inside a run budget (observatory.run_budget_s, 240 s), and a site the budget did not reach is stored as not graded — budget ran out, never left on its previous grade; the deep-monitor sweep keeps a budget of its own (monitor.sweep_budget_s, 120 s) and records every probe it did not reach as unknown with the reason; the sidecar drains the syslog receiver before the actions as well as after them, and prints slow action: … took N s for anything over 60 s so the journal names what held the tick.
          • satom get system health graded the disk at a fixed 80 % / 90 % while the console graded the same filesystem from Settings → Thresholds (80 / 92). /healthz now reports the node's effective host limits (numbers only) and the CLI reads them from there; when it cannot, it says the limits are the shipped defaults instead of implying they came from Settings.
          • The syslog receiver's card and manual say what the setting does not do: switching it on opens a socket, not the node's packet filter — the operator allows the port from the appliances' management networks on every node, primary and standby (a1's own in-container ruleset dropped the datagrams on 2026-10-21 while receiver, parser and attribution all worked).
          • A SATOM node's disk read about 4 points emptier than it was. The percentage was used ÷ total, which counts the ~5 % ext4 keeps for root; PostgreSQL and SATOM do not run as root. On a1 it read 77.7 % while df and satom get system health read 82 %, and the 92 % critical, meant to fire before PostgreSQL can no longer write WAL, would have fired at 97 % of what PostgreSQL can write. It is now df's figure (used ÷ used + free), and the node tile shows used and free space.
          • The SATOM nodes' CPU alert could never fire. Settings → Thresholds → SATOM machine still held the load-average limits (150 % / 400 % of cores) after the grader moved to the container's own CPU use on 2026-08-11, and that reading never goes above 100 %, so a node pinned at 100 % graded OK. The limits are now CPU busy — warning / critical, 80 % / 95 %, validated as percentages; a value above 100 saved under the old meaning is read as the default. Found while drawing those limits on the new Resource history chart.
          • The Wiki list's page 2 and later kept only the first ticked ADOM of the filter.
          • The offline installer, measured on a bare Debian 12 container (an install of 2.11.0 from its bundle, done to rehearse the upgrade path to this release) needed four workarounds, each a defect in installers/ that every release since carried:
          • The guided installer died on "curl is missing" although the bundle next to it carried curl and an offline install has no package manager to fetch it with. It now installs curl from the bundle; the online path keeps the check. Its --help also promised SETUP_EXISTING=update for a native install that only accepts reinstall|abort (an update is an update package); the help now says what the installer does.
          • Forcing the bundle's whole dependency closure with dpkg -i upgraded libsystemd0, libudev1 and libpam-modules over an older point release and pulled libelogind0 in as an alternative provider — "unmet dependencies: systemd, udev, libpam-modules-bin", the install aborted halfway with no network to repair it. The installer now installs only what the image lacks, never replaces a base package that is present, and the bundle builder leaves the alternative providers out and records the closure it resolved (bundle/debs-closure.txt).
          • On an image whose locale is C the PostgreSQL cluster is SQL_ASCII and a plain createdb inherited it; psycopg then returned bytes and flask create-db died two steps later under a hint that blamed authentication. The database is now created UTF8 from template0 with the C locale on every distribution, an existing database that is not UTF8 is refused with its encoding named, and the hint names both causes.
          • nginx never read the vhost: the Debian package had started it with the distro's default site before the vhost existed, enable --now is a no-op on a running service, and the readiness check then failed on an install that was otherwise complete. The installer restarts nginx after writing the vhost (a restart, not a reload — the openSUSE $MAINPID race stays closed).
          • The documented upgrade path for a node on 3.3.2 or older did not work as written. Those nodes run an update runner that points pip at a staging directory only root can read, so the first package that ships a wheel the venv lacks — the prescribed satom-update-3.3.3.tar.gz included — fails at pip install and rolls back cleanly, every time; the runner that fixed it (3.3.3) is inside the very package it cannot apply. The release notes and the update manual now give the step that works: install the package's own runner first (deploy/install-runner.sh from the verified package, as root), then apply the package. Measured on a 2.11.0 node: the first apply rolled back, the second — after that step — upgraded to 3.3.3 with the data intact.
